name: Regional Development Institutions
description: Iran’s regional development framework connects provincial planning organizations with national planning authorities and provincial decision-making councils. The documents inspected distinguish technical preparation, approval, and implementation responsibilities rather than assigning regional development to a single institution. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Regional Development Institutions in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand the documented roles of Iran’s provincial planning organizations, national planning authorities, and development councils.

content.heading: A technical organization within each province
content.content:
A useful starting point is the provincial Management and Planning Organization, known in Persian as the *Sazman-e Modiriyat va Barnamerizi*. A 1393 Solar Hijri reorganization, corresponding to 2014, provided for these organizations to be separated from provincial governorates. Its remit covered planning, budgeting, management development, human resources, technical affairs, and supervision within national policy. [s1]

The same resolution connected provincial and national authority: the governor proposed the organization’s head, while the national organization’s head approved and issued the appointment. The governor could refer economic, social, and cultural studies and planning matters to the organization. This arrangement helps explain why technical planning and political coordination should be examined separately, even when they work closely together. These are provisions of the historical resolution, not verification of every appointment procedure at the research cutoff. [s1]

content.heading: How national planning shapes regional work
content.content:
A subsequent administrative resolution in 1395 Solar Hijri, corresponding to 2016, separated national administrative and employment affairs from planning and budget affairs. It assigned the Plan and Budget Organization responsibilities including development strategies, annual budget preparation, monitoring, statistics coordination, and spatial planning. [s2]

Spatial planning—*amayesh-e sarzamin* in Persian—concerns the geographic organization of development. Article 32 of the Permanent Provisions of Development Programs Law establishes a national spatial-planning council with responsibilities spanning national, regional, and provincial plans. Its provisions require executive agencies to align operational programs with spatial-planning directions. Regional development therefore sits within a national framework, rather than being solely a provincial choice. [s3]

content.heading: From planning work to decisions
content.content:
The provincial planning organization also hosts the secretariat of the provincial Planning and Development Council. Under the inspected implementing regulation, the secretariat prepares council business, follows decisions, and assembles performance reporting. Specialist working groups develop proposals for council consideration. This provides an institutional bridge between technical work and collective decisions. [s4]

For readers assessing a development announcement, the practical question is which stage the evidence establishes. A study, a council decision, and a completed investment require different records. The inspected organizational documents explain responsibilities; they do not demonstrate delivery or establish that regional inequalities have narrowed.

name: Provincial Planning Councils
description: Iran’s provincial Planning and Development Councils bring together officials to consider development plans, investment priorities, and specified provincial budget matters. The inspected legal framework gives the governor the chair and the provincial planning organization’s head the secretarial role. [s1]

seo.title: Iran’s Provincial Planning Councils | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the documented responsibilities of provincial Planning and Development Councils, their secretariats, and specialist working groups.

content.heading: A forum for provincial development decisions
content.content:
The institution usually shortened here to a provincial planning council is the *Shora-ye Barnamerizi va Tose'e-ye Ostan*, or Provincial Planning and Development Council. Article 31 of the Permanent Provisions of Development Programs Law describes it as the highest provincial decision-making and supervisory body for economic, social, and cultural development. Its responsibilities nevertheless operate within national planning and policy constraints. [s1]

The council considers provincial development documents, monitors balanced development, and addresses investment coordination. Its membership brings the governor and planning organization together with provincial officials; parliamentary representatives participate as observers. This is an administrative development council, and its statutory responsibilities should not be confused with those of an elected municipal council. [s1]

content.heading: The boundary between province and county
content.content:
Article 31 limits the council’s role in the specified county allocations: it determines county totals for capital-asset appropriations and the referenced balanced-development funding using population and deprivation indicators. The provision expressly bars interference in county planning committee decisions. This distinction matters when identifying which body is responsible for a particular allocation. [s1]

The implementing regulation also assigns the council consideration of provincial operating-budget distribution and policies for selecting provincial capital projects. These provisions concern defined public-budget responsibilities; they do not establish control over every investment made within a province. [s2]

content.heading: How proposals reach the council
content.content:
The inspected regulation organizes specialist work around economic affairs and investment; infrastructure, settlements, spatial planning and environment; social affairs and health; and education, research and innovation. Working-group decisions are proposals requiring council approval under the relevant rules. The secretariat follows implementation and prepares periodic performance reports. [s2]

This distinction provides a useful way to read meeting reports: a working-group recommendation and a council approval represent different stages. Neither, by itself, proves that expenditure occurred or a project was completed.

content.title: Documented proposal and follow-up relationships
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Specialist working groups"] -->|"Submit proposals"| B["Provincial planning secretariat"]
  B -->|"Prepares council business"| C["Planning and Development Council"]
  C -->|"Decisions communicated to relevant bodies"| D["Provincial executive agencies"]
  B -->|"Follows decisions and reports performance"| C
  E["Provincial planning organization"] -->|"Hosts"| B
```
content.summary: The diagram summarizes the inspected regulation. Proposal preparation, council decisions, and follow-up are distinct relationships; the diagram does not certify implementation.

name: Electoral System
description: Iran’s electoral framework combines popular voting with institutional supervision and restrictions on candidacy. Understanding it requires distinguishing the offices being elected, the administration of voting, and the unelected authorities that constrain electoral competition. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Iran’s Electoral System: Voting and Institutional Limits | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iran’s elected institutions, presidential voting rules, election administration, candidate screening, and participation.

content.heading: Different elections choose different institutions
content.content:
Iran’s elections should be understood as several distinct contests. The presidency heads the executive except in matters assigned directly to the leadership. Parliament, commonly called the *Majles*, is the national legislature. The Assembly of Experts has a different function: it selects and constitutionally oversees the Supreme Leader. Elections to these bodies do not confer identical powers. [s1][s2]

The House of Commons Library’s account of the March 2024 elections describes a parliament elected for four-year terms and an Assembly of Experts elected for eight-year terms. Both were elected that March, but their different functions make their results separate political questions. Local councils form another branch of the electoral landscape; their role should be examined through the specific council framework rather than inferred from national election rules. [s2][s1]

content.heading: The constitutional presidential rules
content.content:
The Constitution provides for direct presidential election to a four-year term, with only one immediately consecutive reelection. A candidate must obtain an absolute majority of votes cast. If nobody does, Article 117 provides for a second round between the leading candidates, subject to its withdrawal provisions. Article 115 sets qualifications including nationality, administrative ability, and adherence to the Islamic Republic and its official religious school. [s1]

These rules describe selection for an office whose authority has constitutional boundaries. Winning the presidency does not transfer the powers assigned to the Supreme Leader or remove the other institutions that supervise and constrain elected government. [s1][s3]

content.heading: Who administers and who supervises?
content.content:
Article 99 assigns the Guardian Council supervision of presidential, parliamentary, and Assembly of Experts elections, as well as referendums. Its composition combines Islamic-law specialists selected by the Supreme Leader with jurists elected by parliament from nominees of the judiciary’s head. [s1]

Election administration involves a separate apparatus. The parliamentary electoral-law translation inspected at Syracuse University assigns implementation roles to the Interior Ministry and provincial, county, and district authorities. It also describes executive and supervisory boards. This establishes an important institutional distinction: organizing polling and exercising supervisory authority are separate responsibilities. The translation is useful for understanding that architecture, but its detailed thresholds and procedures should not be treated as a consolidated statement of law effective in 2026. [s4]

content.heading: Voting within a restricted candidate field
content.content:
Freedom House’s report covering 2024 assesses Iran’s elections as failing international democratic standards. It identifies Guardian Council screening as a central restriction: voters choose among candidates admitted to the contest, while political actors outside the establishment face substantial barriers. This is an independent assessment of electoral practice, distinct from the Constitution’s description of institutions. [s3]

The March 2024 parliamentary and Assembly of Experts contests illustrate the difference. The Commons Library records the exclusion of reformist and moderate candidates, including former president Hassan Rouhani from the Assembly contest. It also reports the Guardian Council’s explanation that most rejected Assembly candidates failed education-related criteria. Reporting both the institutional explanation and the observed narrowing of competition helps readers distinguish stated grounds from their political consequences. [s2]

The presidential election later in 2024 followed Ebrahim Raisi’s death and proceeded to a runoff in which Masoud Pezeshkian defeated Saeed Jalili. Freedom House records both that electoral outcome and substantial restrictions on the candidate field. Competition among approved candidates and restrictions on entry can therefore coexist. [s3]

content.heading: How to interpret participation
content.content:
Freedom House describes low turnout in the 2024 national contests and connects it with public disillusionment. Such interpretation should remain attributed: an aggregate turnout figure cannot identify every abstaining voter’s motivation. Parliamentary elections and presidential rounds also represent different events, so their participation figures should retain their election type and round rather than be combined into a single annual observation. [s3]

The linked pages separate presidential elections, parliamentary elections, local councils, electoral law, participation, and administration. Together, these questions provide a more useful reading of an election than the winner’s name alone: which office was contested, who could stand, who ran the process, and what evidence supports judgments about participation and fairness?
